summary: Defines metrics for the pattern of packet loss on a one-way Internet path, not just the overall loss rate. Two paths with equal loss rates can feel very different to users of real-time voice and video if their losses are bursty.

eli5.summary: Losing ten words in a row sounds worse than losing one word ten times. These measurements describe how losses are spread out, not only how many happen.

questions: how to measure packet loss patterns
why does bursty packet loss matter
subtitle: Metrics that capture the pattern and burstiness of packet loss, not just the rate

tldr.problem: Simple packet loss rate does not reveal the user experience impact: two paths with the same loss rate feel very different if one loses packets randomly while the other loses many packets in a row (bursts).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two derived metrics called loss distance (the spacing between lost packets) and loss period (groups of consecutive loss events), along with statistics that characterize the burstiness and distribution of losses.
tldr.outcome: Applications and network operators can now distinguish between scattered losses and bursty losses, allowing better understanding of voice, video, and TCP performance, and more accurate quality assessment.

facts.label: Application examples
facts.value: Voice over IP, Video streaming, TCP throughput analysis

today: RFC 3357 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. It remains the specification for loss pattern metrics in the IPPM framework, used by network operators and application developers to characterize one-way path behavior beyond simple loss rate.

sections.title: The Problem of Loss Rate Alone
sections.content:
For real-time applications like voice over IP and video streaming, the distribution of packet losses is as important as the loss rate itself. A stream with 1 percent loss where all losses occur in one burst (losing 100 consecutive packets out of 10,000 total) creates a noticeable glitch in audio or video, whereas the same 1 percent loss rate with losses scattered evenly throughout the stream causes only minor degradation that perceptual codecs can conceal.

The loss pattern or loss distribution determines perceived performance, yet the basic one-way loss metric defined in RFC 2680 provides only an overall loss rate. This document builds on that base metric by defining derived metrics that capture packet loss patterns: how far apart the losses are (loss distance), and how many consecutive losses occur together (loss period and burstiness).
sections.eli5: The loss rate tells you how many packets do not arrive. But the loss pattern tells you whether they are spread out or clumped together. For speech and video, clumped losses sound or look worse.

sections.title: Loss Distance and Loss Period
sections.content:
The RFC defines two main derived metrics. Loss distance is the difference in sequence numbers between two successive lost packets, capturing how far apart losses are. For example, if packet 20 is lost followed by packet 50, the loss distance is 30. Loss period is a counter that increments each time a new burst of losses begins (whenever a lost packet follows a received packet). Loss period groups lost packets into bursts: all packets in one burst belong to the same loss period.

The RFC provides examples showing how these metrics work. In a sequence of received (r) and lost (x) packets like "r r r x r r x x x r x r r x x x", there are four distinct loss periods: one at packet 3, one starting at packet 6 (three consecutive losses), one at packet 10, and one at packet 13. Loss distances show 30, 2, 2, 1 between successive losses, revealing how spread out they are.
sections.eli5: Loss distance is how many good packets are between two lost packets. Loss period is a number for each burst of losses. If you have four separate times when packets get lost, you have four loss periods.

sections.title: Methodology and Sampling
sections.content:
The metrics are derived from the base one-way loss metric by applying the same measurement methodology: synchronized clocks at source and destination, test packets of a specified type (Type-P), and a determination of loss based on whether each packet arrives within a threshold time. The RFC notes that the proposed metrics work with any sampling method, but recommends different sampling strategies for different application types.

For real-time applications like voice over IP, an ON-OFF model may be more appropriate than Poisson sampling, as it better reflects bursty traffic patterns. For TCP-based applications, other models exist that capture TCP's behavior. The key point is that loss distance and loss period are flexible: they characterize whatever loss pattern the underlying base loss metric reveals, without requiring a specific sampling approach.
sections.eli5: To measure these patterns, you send test packets and track which ones get lost. You can send them at different rates or patterns depending on what you want to test, like testing real-time voice or web downloads.

sections.title: Statistical Measures and Applications
sections.content:
The RFC defines four key statistics. Loss-Noticeable-Rate counts losses that occur closer together than a threshold delta; a multimedia codec might set delta based on its ability to conceal losses from nearby history. Loss-Period-Total is simply the number of distinct loss bursts. Loss-Period-Lengths counts how many packets are lost in each burst, revealing burstiness: one burst of 100 consecutive losses has much more impact than 100 single isolated losses. Inter-Loss-Period-Lengths measures the distance between loss bursts, indicating how much time an application has to recover or rebuild state between bursts.

These statistics help network operators understand path quality beyond simple loss rate, and help application developers tune their error concealment and recovery strategies. For example, a multimedia codec facing longer inter-loss-period gaps can maintain better history and achieve better quality despite the same overall loss rate as a codec facing short gaps.
sections.eli5: These statistics tell you: how many losses are close together, how many burst groups there are, how many packets each burst loses, and how far apart the bursts are. Together they tell you if you are dealing with scattered losses or a few big meltdowns.

sections.title: Measurement Considerations and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that conducting Internet measurements raises security and privacy concerns. While these metrics do not themselves specify an implementation, any implementation must be careful not to perturb the network under test. The sending rate (lambda) must be set appropriately to avoid causing congestion or acting as a denial of service attack. Test packets should contain no user data, so privacy is not a concern, but integrity checks using cryptographic hashes may be appropriate to prevent adversaries from corrupting or spoofing test packets.

Additionally, measurement aspects like packet size, loss threshold, and measurement infrastructure choice all influence the accuracy of the metrics. Those interpreting results must account for these factors, and the RFC references the base loss metric (RFC 2680) for detailed treatment of measurement errors and uncertainties.
sections.eli5: Measuring network losses must be done carefully so you do not disrupt the network. The measurements themselves are just data, not user information, but they need to be protected from being faked by attackers.
